//: Entries of depth.py's list that have been read against upstream, with what
the reading found. depth.py hides these unless --all is passed.
The point is that depth.py over-reports by design -- its docstring says so
-- and an over-report that nobody records gets re-read every few ticks.
This file is the difference between a screen and a work queue.
A row belongs here once somebody has compared the type against upstream
member by member and can say why the shortfall is not a gap. `finding` is
that reason, and it has to be checkable: name the mechanism that answers
for the missing members, not just 'looked, fine'. If the reading found a
real gap, the row goes in after the gap is closed, and `finding` says so.
`at` points at where the reasoning lives, so a later reader can check it
rather than take this file's word.

examined.finding: Three families, each answered by a documented architectural choice rather than missing. (1) The in-place mutation machinery -- _replaceChildren, _adoptChild, _dropChild, attach, detach, _markDirty, _redepthChildren, _updateChildMergeFlagRecursively, visitChildren -- has no counterpart because this port rebuilds the tree and diffs it against what was last sent, rather than keeping long-lived nodes and marking them dirty. (2) Upstream splits the id space at (1 << 16) - 1 so framework ids cannot collide with engine ids; this port partitions it into three explicit ranges (AUTO_BASE, TEXT_BASE) for the same purpose. (3) isInvisible's `transform.isZero()` clause is absent because geometry here is a rectangle rather than a matrix, so a collapsing transform arrives as an empty rect and the first clause catches it.
examined.at: src/flutter/rust/rustflutter/src/semantics.rs -- SemanticsOwner's doc comment for (1), take_text_id and TEXT_BASE for (2), SemanticsNode::is_invisible for (3)

examined.finding: Twenty-one of upstream's twenty-four members are optional callback fields, which are Dart wiring rather than behaviour. The behaviour is in the state that routes gestures to them, and reading it found a real gap: _getEffectiveConsecutiveTapCount was missing entirely, along with the routing rules that consume it. Ported, with the three platform arithmetics. reports_tap was also fixed -- it had misread onUserTap's condition as 'the tap changed something' rather than 'the first tap of a series'.

Four of upstream's six public members are State lifecycle (initState, dispose, didUpdateWidget, build), which this port has no counterpart for by construction. The other two, open and close, were a real gap and are now ported -- along with the back-button state machine they drive, which is the part worth having: the local history entry is managed on the forward and reverse statuses, both of which are the moments the drawer STARTS moving, while completed and dismissed do nothing at all.

A constructor facade: `pub struct Listener;` whose new() returns RenderPointerRegion, so the members are counted on neither. Checked field by field rather than assumed. Upstream declares nine callbacks plus behavior; PointerHandlers carries all nine -- down, move, up, cancel, the pan-zoom trio, on_scroll for onPointerSignal, and both halves of hovering (on_hover_change for enter/leave and on_hover for the move stream) -- and behavior lives on RenderPointerRegion with a with_behavior builder. Nothing missing.

The same facade shape, over RenderParagraph -- which is also what `pub type Text = RenderParagraph` names, and depth.py now scores that alias at 40 members against upstream Text's 18. RichText is measured against the identical body, so the 2 of 16 was the facade and not the port.
examined.at: src/flutter/rust/rustflutter/src/widgets.rs -- RichText::new returns RenderParagraph; `pub type Text = RenderParagraph` on the same file

examined.finding: A constructor facade over RenderImage, and the reading found real gaps rather than dismissing the entry. Upstream declares scale, color, colorBlendMode and filterQuality beyond what RenderImage carried; width and height are answered by `size` and debugImageLabel is debug ceremony. scale landed in tick 124, color and colorBlendMode here -- the latter needed a new rf_paint_set_color_filter in the FFI, because a tint is ColorFilter.mode(colour, srcIn) and not a blend mode on the paint. filterQuality remains open: it is a sampling hint on the draw call rather than on the paint, and nothing in the crate has a place to put it yet.
examined.at: src/flutter/rust/rustflutter/src/render.rs -- RenderImage::with_scale, with_colour, effective_blend_mode, source_rect; painting.rs -- Paint::with_color_filter; src/flutter/rust/ffi/rustflutter_ffi.cc -- rf_paint_set_color_filter

examined.finding: Read against upstream's member list, and the reading found the port refusing merges upstream allows. isCompatibleWith here had two clauses upstream does not have -- hintOverrides and indexInParent -- so a config carrying either would be split into a second node where upstream folds it into one, which a reader hears as an extra stop. Upstream asks only about platformViewId, maxValueLength, currentValueLength, attributedValue, minValue and maxValue, every one of them something a render object says about itself; a hint override and a position in a parent come from an ancestor, and absorb keeps the outer one by first-wins. Both clauses removed. accessibilityFocusBlockType was added because its merge -- the one strongest-wins rule in the class -- was already written and tested in this crate with no field carrying it, so the rule could never be reached. The bigger fact, now in the type's doc comment: absorb and isCompatibleWith have no caller outside the tests. The walk runs on SemanticsAnnotation, which is why the two wrong rules survived. Still open, all of them merge rules rather than fields: controlsNodes unions rather than first-wins; validationResult has invalid always taking precedence; hitTestBehavior refuses a merge when EITHER side is non-defer, not when both are set; role and inputType use `none` as their unset the way headingLevel uses 0 and identifier uses ''.
examined.at: src/flutter/rust/rustflutter/src/semantics.rs -- SemanticsConfiguration::is_compatible_with (the two removed clauses and why), ::absorb (the strongest-wins line), accessibility_focus_block_type, and the type's "Nothing in the walk calls these yet" section

examined.finding: The 3/46 is mostly a class-shape artefact: this port merges the three control tiles into one ControlListTile plus one ControlTile, which is documented on both, so the members depth.py counts on SwitchListTile live elsewhere. Read upstream's 55 members: all but six are constructor fields forwarded to Switch or ListTile. Of the six that carry rules, effectiveControlAffinity and the .adaptive path were already here. Two were not. (1) selectedColor: effectiveActiveColor -- upstream's three tiles all hand their ListTile a selected colour taken from their own control, so a selected row is drawn in the colour of the thing that made it selected. This port resolved it from the list tile theme alone, which puts the theme's accent on a row whose switch is some other colour: two accents on one line. Added, with ListTile::with_selected_color and ResolvedListTile::of_with_selected_color. (2) ExcludeFocus around the control -- upstream wraps it so the tile is the focusable thing and tabbing a settings page stops once per row rather than twice. NOT added: neither the controls nor ListTile register a focus node in this port, so wrapping would model a rule with no mechanism behind it. Also open and recorded in list_tiles.rs: the line handing the colour to the tile is not covered, because a ListTile's resolved text colour is not observable -- Drawn::Paragraph records text and position but not colour. Recording the style's colour in the paragraph stub would close that and every other text-colour claim in the crate.
examined.at: src/flutter/rust/rustflutter/src/component_themes.rs -- ResolvedListTile::of_with_selected_color; components.rs -- ListTile::with_selected_color; list_tiles.rs -- ControlTile::control_active_color and the control_colour_tests module

examined.finding: Read against upstream's label rules, which are the ones this class carries beyond its forwarded fields: _labelShouldWithdraw, labelShouldWithdraw, _floatingLabelEnabled, _hasInlineLabel and _shouldShowLabel. Two were wrong here. (1) _shouldShowLabel is `_hasInlineLabel || _floatingLabelEnabled`, false in exactly one case: behaviour `never` with the label withdrawn. It has nowhere to go -- never forbids the floating position and the reader's text is in the inline one. This port had no such state and answered Inline, which draws the label ON TOP OF WHAT WAS TYPED. LabelPlacement::Hidden added. (2) _labelShouldWithdraw is `!isEmpty || (isFocused && decoration.enabled)`, and the enabled term was missing: a disabled field that holds focus floated its label, saying it was being edited when it cannot be. FloatingLabelBehavior now splits withdraws() from allows_floating(), which is upstream's own split and the reason the two questions are not the same one: a label withdraws because something is in the field, and floats only if the behaviour lets it. Still forwarded rather than modelled, and not a gap: the ~40 style, colour and constraint fields, which reach the InputDecorationTheme this crate already resolves. Tick 179 read the rest: upstream asserts SIX 'only one of' pairs and this had three -- the doc even said 'three'. The label, hint and error pairs were missing, and so were the widget forms they are about. _hasError is `errorText != null || error != null`, so a field given an error widget reported no error at all: its subtitle line stayed on the helper and its border stayed the enabled colour. A label given as a widget was Absent, so it never floated. has_error(), has_label() and hint_text added, with the three missing asserts.

Read member by member and closed for content, not for shape. Upstream spells eight static methods -- vibrate, lightImpact, mediumImpact, heavyImpact, selectionClick, successNotification, warningNotification, errorNotification -- and all eight put the SAME method name on the wire (`HapticFeedback.vibrate`); only the argument differs. So they are one function and an eight-value enum here, and depth.py, which counts symbols by name, will keep reporting 2/8 forever. It is counting a spelling difference. Tick 184 added the three notification kinds, which were genuinely absent -- an application could not ask for a success, warning or error haptic at all, and on iOS those three are a different generator (UINotificationFeedbackGenerator) from the impacts rather than the same thing at another weight. The five payload strings that were already here were unchanged. Nothing remains: every upstream method has a variant.

Twenty-nine of upstream's thirty members are answered somewhere in the crate, and checking them one at a time against the WHOLE crate rather than against the type named after it is what showed that: ButtonTextTheme, MaterialButtonColors (getTextColor, getDisabledTextColor, getFillColor and its runtime-type clause), MaterialTapTargetSize, RawMaterialButton and ButtonElevations between them carry the colours, the five elevations, the constraints and the tap target. Exactly one had no reader anywhere: colorBrightness, upstream's getBrightness -- `button.colorBrightness ?? colorScheme.brightness`. text_color already took a brightness, so the machinery was complete and the override that feeds it was absent; a button with a dark custom fill on a light page had no way to say so and ButtonTextTheme::Normal gave it a black label. Ported. It reaches exactly one of the three text themes: Normal asks the brightness directly, Primary asks the fill first and only falls back to it, Accent never asks -- which is why nothing noticed.

The ratio will not move and should not. This port has ONE ControlListTile where upstream has three widgets (RadioListTile, CheckboxListTile, SwitchListTile), so members answered for all three are counted against none of them. Reading the list found four real gaps, all ported: `enabled` as a bool? whose assert is asymmetric (it may turn a tile off freely and may only turn one on where a handler or a RadioGroup already exists); `toggleable`, which upstream declares IS the tristate (`bool get tristate => widget.toggleable`); the tap rule, where a plain radio already chosen SWALLOWS the tap rather than reporting the same value again; and radioScaleFactor, whose one is `no wrapper at all` rather than a scale of one. The state properties radioBackgroundColor/radioSide/radioInnerRadius remain unported and wait on these tiles drawing their own control rather than assembling ListTile slots.
examined.at: src/flutter/rust/rustflutter/src/list_tiles.rs -- ControlListTile::is_enabled, validate_enabled, tap_on_radio, with_toggleable, scales_the_control, draws_a_cupertino_checkmark

examined.finding: Most of upstream's seventy-three fields are answered outside the widget: editable_text.rs carries read_only, enable_interactive_selection and the editing state; services/text_formatter.rs carries maxLength, MaxLengthEnforcement and its platform table (with a recorded divergence -- grapheme clusters upstream, scalar values here); services/text_input.rs carries the keyboard types and actions. What was genuinely absent was the CONSTRUCTOR itself: eight asserts and three derived defaults, none of them present. Five of the eight are about pairs of fields rather than one value's range, and each carries its own message. Ported, with the two that are easy to get wrong written down: noMaxLength is -1 and legal (counter, no limit) rather than 'any negative', and an obscured field both refuses to be multiline and turns smart punctuation off by default -- an IME turning `--` into an em-dash silently changes a password to something unreadable and unrepeatable.

Same cause as RadioListTile -- this port has one ControlListTile where upstream has three widgets -- and checking each of upstream's forty-one members against the whole crate left five with no hit, one of which (_checkboxType) is the private adaptive marker already carried as `adaptive`. Three of the four real ones are ported here. checkboxShape: the box falls through CheckboxThemeData.shape to RoundedRectangleBorder(circular 1.0) -- ONE, not the usual four, so a checkbox is a square with its corners barely taken off. checkboxScaleFactor: the same field the radio has, and the shared one is named by the fact that SwitchListTile has NEITHER a scale factor nor a shape -- a switch has nothing to scale independently of its track, and the two controls that draw a mark inside a box do. internalAddSemanticForOnTap: whether a tappable row says button:true to a screen reader, which upstream's own doc calls 'a temporary flag to help changing the behavior of ListTile onTap semantics' -- and it is only half the condition, since upstream adds the flag *if onTap is provided*. The fourth, checkboxSemanticLabel, waits on these tiles describing their control separately from their row, which is what radioBackgroundColor and its two neighbours wait on too.

Worked through over ticks 273-281, and the low ratio is a shape difference rather than a gap. This port keeps RenderEditable narrow and answers its behaviour in named types beside it, each with its own tests: WordSelection (getWordAtOffset, selectWordEdge, selectWordsInRange), FloatingCursor (setFloatingCursor, calculateBoundedFloatingCursorOffset, floatingCursorAddedMargin), CaretGeometry and CaretRect (paintCursorAboveText, cursorRadius, cursorOffset, cursorOpacityAnimates, _computeCaretPrototype, getLocalRectForCaret, _kCaretHeightOffset), SelectionEndpoints and SelectionVisibility (getEndpointsForSelection, _updateSelectionExtentsVisibility, selectionStartInViewport, selectionEndInViewport), FieldExtent (_preferredHeight, _adjustConstraints, _caretMargin, _kCaretGap, the four intrinsics, _countHardLineBreaks), ComposingRegion (getRectForComposingRange, _snapToPhysicalPixel), TextHighlightPainter with EditablePainters (_TextHighlightPainter, setPromptRectRange, promptRectColor, the two built-in painter stacks), and VerticalCaretMovementRun with VerticalCaretStep (getTextPositionAbove, getTextPositionBelow, moveByOffset). What genuinely has no counterpart is the in-place render object machinery -- attach, detach, redepthChildren, defaultApplyPaintTransform, layoutInlineChildren, paintInlineChildren, positionInlineChildren, hitTestInlineChildren, systemFontsDidChange -- because this port rebuilds and diffs rather than keeping long-lived nodes, the same reason recorded for SemanticsNode; and the LayerLink pair (startHandleLayerLink, endHandleLayerLink), because handles are positioned from endpoints here rather than by following a leader layer. Reasoning in PORTING_STATUS.md ticks 273-281.

The drag lifecycle -- isDraggingStartHandle, isDraggingEndHandle, the six onStartHandleDrag*/onEndHandleDrag* callbacks, _canDragStartHandle and the two flags behind each handle -- is ported as HandleDragState beside SelectionOverlay rather than on it, with its own tests, which is why the ratio does not move. The three LayerLink fields (startHandleLayerLink, endHandleLayerLink, toolbarLayerLink) have no counterpart for the reason recorded for RenderEditable: this port positions handles and toolbar from computed endpoints rather than by following leader layers. capturedThemes and debugRequiredFor belong to Overlay's inherited-widget plumbing, which this port does not have. Reasoning in PORTING_STATUS.md tick 282.

A mapping difference plus four ticks of real work, and the ratio counts neither. depth pairs upstream's `Route` with `navigation::Route`, which is a name and some arguments -- upstream's `RouteSettings`, not its `Route`. The lifecycle object the ratio is really asking about is `routes.rs`, spread over `OverlayRoute`/`TransitionRoute`/`ModalRoute` the way upstream spreads it over the same subclasses: install, didPush, didPop, didPopNext, dispose, willHandlePopInternally and popDisposition were already there. Ticks 478-482 closed what was genuinely missing: the four position questions (isCurrent, isFirst, isActive, hasActiveRouteBelow) over `RoutePosition` with the `_RouteLifecycle` ranges they need; didReplace, didChangeNext, didChangePrevious, changedInternalState and changedExternalState with the content upstream's subclasses give them; and popped / currentResult / didComplete as `RouteCompletion`, wired through `HistoryEntry::handle_pop` and `handle_complete` and then into the running stack's pop, replace and pop_to_root.
examined.at: src/flutter/rust/rustflutter/src/routes.rs (RoutePosition, RouteLifecycle, HistoryEntry, RouteCompletion) and src/navigation.rs; PORTING_STATUS.md ticks 478-482.

examined.finding: The overlay half of upstream's controller is `magnifier_host::MagnifierHost`, which `magnifier.rs`'s own module docs say outright: it holds the entry, moves it as the gesture moves, hides it, and takes it down -- overlayEntry, show, hide(removeFromOverlay:), removeFromOverlay and shown all answer there. `MagnifierController` keeps only shiftWithinBounds, which is the part that is a rule rather than a lifetime. Reading it member by member at tick 483 found one real gap and closed it: `shown`'s second half, `animationController?.isForwardOrCompleted ?? true` -- a loupe animating out is already not shown, and one with no entry animation is shown as soon as it exists.
examined.at: src/flutter/rust/rustflutter/src/magnifier_host.rs (MagnifierHost::is_shown, animation_status, hide) and the module docs at the top of src/magnifier.rs; PORTING_STATUS.md tick 483.

examined.finding: Zero of upstream's seventeen `on*` callbacks share a name with anything in this crate, and all seventeen rules are present under other names: onSingleTapUp/onDoubleTapDown/onTripleTapDown are single_tap_up, double_tap_down and multi_tap_down; the four onSingleLongTap* are long_press_start/move_update/end/finish; onDragSelectionStart/Update/End are drag_selection_*; onForcePressStart/End, onSecondaryTap and onSecondaryTapDown keep their shape; the shift arms are shift_tap_down and shift_drag_update. This port models them as rule functions over a `SingleTapContext` rather than as callbacks on a builder, which is why the names do not line up. Reading it at tick 484 found one real gap and closed it: onTapTrackStart/onTapTrackReset and the `_isShiftPressed` they maintain -- the keyboard is sampled once when the tap track begins, and every shift rule in the file is handed that value rather than reading the keyboard itself.
examined.at: src/flutter/rust/rustflutter/src/text_selection.rs (TapTrackShift, and the shift_* rules it feeds); PORTING_STATUS.md tick 484.

examined.finding: A generated table of codepoints, and the decision not to copy it is recorded where it was taken: `icons.rs`'s module docs say upstream's file is 29,454 lines holding 8,825 `static const IconData` declarations, all of it between `// BEGIN GENERATED ICONS` and `// Generated code: do not hand-edit.`, and that nine thousand codepoints add nothing a reader could not get from the font itself. What has anything to say is the machinery -- `MaterialIcon` with its `matchTextDirection`, the direction rule, the platform-adaptive lookup -- and that is ported, with a representative handful of icons to exercise it. The count itself is recorded as `Icons::UPSTREAM_ICON_COUNT`, so the shortfall is a number in the source rather than an omission. This ratio can only be closed by pasting the generated block, which would move the ratio and nothing else; it stays at the head of the list for ever otherwise.

The same generated-table reading as `Icons`, on the Cupertino side: 1,322 codepoints, recorded as `CupertinoIcons::UPSTREAM_ICON_COUNT` rather than reproduced, with a test that holds it against Material's 8,825. This crate has no icon font at all -- `cupertino.rs`'s module docs lead with it -- so the glyphs the widgets actually need are *drawn* (`BackChevron`, `SearchGlyph`, `ClearGlyph`), which is why those exist as render objects and the codepoints do not.
examined.at: src/flutter/rust/rustflutter/src/cupertino_controls.rs (CupertinoIcons::UPSTREAM_ICON_COUNT and the test beside it); the 'No icon font' note at the top of src/cupertino.rs.
